acts.intro.152: On the way to Jairus's daughter
acts.note.152:0.desc: When Jesus' boat returned on Tuesday forenoon, a great crowd was waiting, and Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, fell at his feet begging him to heal his only daughter, who was at the point of death. As Jesus went with him, the crowd followed, and near the house a woman touched the hem of his garment.
acts.note.152:0.diff: Matthew says the daughter had just died, whereas The Urantia Book, like Mark and Luke, says she was at the point of death, and adds that new observers from the Sanhedrin were in the crowd.
acts.note.sub:152:0.2–3.desc: In a narrow street on the way to Jairus's house, a woman long afflicted with a hemorrhage touched the hem of Jesus' garment and was healed. Sensing that living energy had gone forth from him, Jesus called her and said her faith had made her whole; touching the garment was merely the superstitious part, and the healing came from faith.
acts.note.sub:152:0.2–3.diff: The Gospels describe an unnamed woman ill for twelve years, whereas The Urantia Book names her Veronica of Caesarea-Philippi and says Jesus did not consciously will the healing and her touching the garment was superstition.
acts.note.152:1.desc: At Jairus's house a servant said the daughter was dead, but Jesus went in with Peter, James, John, and the parents, took the girl by the hand, and bade her awake and arise. He explained that she had been in a coma following a long fever and had not been raised from the dead, but the apostles would not believe it.
acts.note.152:1.diff: The Gospels present the girl as dead and restored to life (Luke says her spirit returned), whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus himself explained that he had only aroused her from a coma.
acts.sub.152:1.3: Two blind men and a dumb boy
acts.note.sub:152:1.3.desc: As Jesus left Jairus's house, two blind men led by a dumb boy followed him, crying out for healing. Jesus' reputation as a healer was then at its height, and he looked so worn that his friends feared he might collapse.
acts.note.sub:152:1.3.diff: Matthew says the two blind men received sight and a dumb demoniac spoke, whereas The Urantia Book says only that they cried out for healing, records no cure, and makes the boy their guide.
acts.map27.head: Up to Jerusalem, and Then to the North
acts.map27.1.head: Across the lake; the five thousand fed
acts.map27.1.body: On Sunday, March 27, they crossed to a park south of Bethsaida-Julias. After the five thousand were fed on Wednesday, the apostles rowed back by night and anchored near Zebedee's house before daylight Thursday (dashed).
acts.map27.2.head: Rest in the region of Gennesaret
acts.map27.2.body: They went by boat for two or three days of rest at the home of a wealthy believer.
acts.map27.3.head: Up to Jerusalem for the Passover
acts.map27.3.body: On Sunday, April 3, they left Bethsaida by way of Gerasa and Philadelphia and arrived at Bethany late on Wednesday evening, April 6.
acts.map27.4.head: Back by the coast cities
acts.map27.4.body: On Sunday, April 24, they left Jerusalem by way of Joppa, Caesarea, and Ptolemais, then overland by Ramah and Chorazin to Bethsaida, arriving on Friday, April 29. The next day he spoke in the Capernaum synagogue.
acts.map27.5.head: Escaping arrest, to near Kheresa
acts.map27.5.body: On Sunday morning, May 22, they rowed over to near Kheresa and spent the night in the park a little way to the north.
acts.map27.6.head: Two weeks at Caesarea-Philippi
acts.map27.6.body: Leaving on Monday, May 23, by way of the Jordan, they arrived on Tuesday, May 24. Peter and the evangelists spent two weeks at Chorazin before joining them.
acts.map27.7.head: By Luz to Sidon
acts.map27.7.body: Leaving on Thursday, June 9, they passed around the marsh country by way of Luz and arrived at Sidon on Friday afternoon.
acts.note.152:2.desc: On Sunday, March 27, Jesus and the apostles crossed to the parks south of Bethsaida-Julias to rest, but the people followed, numbering about five thousand by Wednesday. With the five barley loaves and two fishes held by the Mark lad, Jesus fed the multitude, and the fragments filled twelve baskets.
acts.note.152:2.diff: The Gospels tell it as the events of one day, whereas The Urantia Book places it on the third day, against the background of a plot to make Jesus king, and calls it his first and only consciously preplanned nature miracle.
acts.note.152:3.desc: When the well-fed multitude shouted with one voice to make him king, Jesus stood on a huge stone, declared that his kingdom is not of this world, and told them all to go home. Many departed disappointed, and Jesus asked Andrew to pray for Peter and went alone into the hills.
acts.note.152:3.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus perceived their intent and quietly withdrew into the hills, whereas The Urantia Book says he publicly rebuked the multitude and refused the kingship before going into the hills.
acts.note.152:4.desc: Rowing that night without their Master, the exhausted Peter fell asleep and dreamed that Jesus came walking on the water and that he himself walked on the water and sank. In his dream he actually stepped overboard and awoke as Andrew, James, and John pulled him out, and he always believed the experience was real.
acts.note.152:4.diff: The Gospels say Jesus actually walked on the water, whereas The Urantia Book explains it was Peter's dream and vision, and that Luke regarded it as a vision and left it out of his record.
acts.note.152:5.desc: On Thursday morning Jesus, with the Mark lad, returned to Bethsaida on foot. Of the five thousand only about five hundred still followed him; Jesus gathered the apostles and the women, rebuked them, saying material wonders do not win souls, and then went to Gennesaret to rest.
acts.note.152:6.desc: Resting at the home of a wealthy believer in Gennesaret, Jesus held conferences with the apostles every afternoon. His followers, more than fifty thousand in Galilee alone, shrank in less than a month to under five hundred, and he taught that appeals to feelings are transitory and only the appeal to the indwelling spirit bears fruit.
acts.note.152:6.diff: The Gospels say the sick at Gennesaret were healed by touching his garment, whereas The Urantia Book says only that he rested there and taught the apostles, with no account of healings.
acts.note.152:7.desc: On Sunday, April 3, Jesus set out with only the twelve, going by way of Gerasa and Philadelphia, and reached Bethany on April 6; he forbade public teaching during the Passover. Leaving Jerusalem on April 24, they went through the coast cities and returned to Bethsaida on April 29.
acts.note.153:0.desc: On the Friday evening of their return to Bethsaida and on Sabbath morning, Jesus was deep in thought, eating little and saying almost nothing. Each apostle guessed anxiously at what lay ahead, and Jesus went forth from among his dejected followers to preach in the Capernaum synagogue.
acts.note.153:1.desc: At three o'clock on the Sabbath afternoon the new Capernaum synagogue held fifty-three Pharisees and Sadducees from Jerusalem, more than thirty leaders of nearby synagogues, and Herod's observers. The crisis begun with the feeding of the five thousand ended with this sermon, the turning point of his popularity, and Jairus kept his word to let Jesus speak.
acts.note.153:2.desc: Jesus read warnings from Deuteronomy and Jeremiah and pointed out that the crowds had followed him for bread gained without labor. Pointing to the pot of manna carved on the synagogue lintel, he declared himself the bread of life, and when a Jerusalem teacher asked if he was not Joseph's son, he answered that he and the Father are one.
acts.note.153:2.diff: The Gospel of John presents a dialogue with the crowd in Capernaum, whereas The Urantia Book makes it a formal synagogue sermon before Sanhedrin representatives, opening with readings from Deuteronomy and Jeremiah.
acts.note.153:3.desc: In the after meeting, lasting more than three hours, a Pharisee asked how Jesus could give his flesh to eat, and a Jerusalem spy challenged the failure to wash hands. Jesus rebuked them for making void God's commandment by tradition and declared that what defiles a man is the evil that comes from the heart.
acts.note.153:3.diff: The Gospels set the hand-washing dispute apart from the bread of life discourse, whereas The Urantia Book says both occurred the same day in the after meeting following the Capernaum synagogue sermon.
acts.sub.153:3.2: "Give us your flesh to eat" — flesh and blood
acts.note.sub:153:3.2.desc: A Pharisee, mounting a lampstand, shouted that if Jesus was the bread of life, how could he give his flesh to eat and his blood to drink. Jesus answered that he had not taught them to eat his flesh and blood, but that his life in the flesh was a bestowal of the bread of heaven and men could become spiritually one with him.
acts.note.sub:153:3.2.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus told them to eat his flesh and drink his blood, whereas The Urantia Book has Jesus deny teaching this and explain it as spiritual oneness.
acts.note.sub:153:3.3–6.desc: When a Jerusalem spy charged that Jesus and his apostles ate with unwashed hands, Jesus rebuked the hypocrisy of evading the commandment to honor parents through tradition. What defiles a man, he said, is not what enters the mouth but the evil thoughts, envy, pride, and slander that come from the heart.
acts.note.sub:153:3.3–6.diff: The Gospels make this a separate encounter with Pharisees from Jerusalem and mention Corban, whereas The Urantia Book has a spy ask in the after meeting and adds that Peter later overcame his fear of uncleanness through a dream.
acts.note.153:4.desc: In the after meeting Jesus cast an evil spirit out of a youth brought by a Jerusalem Pharisee, and the Pharisees charged that he did it by the power of Beelzebub. Jesus replied that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, warned of the sin of knowingly blaspheming God, and refused their demand for a predetermined sign.
acts.note.153:4.diff: The Gospels give the sign of Jonah and the saying about the spirit returning with seven others, whereas The Urantia Book says only that no sign would be given except what they would see when the Son of Man departs. Mark adds his family coming to seize him.
acts.note.sub:153:4.1–3.desc: A Jerusalem Pharisee brought a youth possessed of an unruly and rebellious spirit and asked whether Jesus could cast out devils; Jesus commanded the spirit to come out and set a loyal spirit to guard the youth. This was the first case of Jesus casting out an actual evil spirit, and such possession existed only until Pentecost.
acts.note.sub:153:4.1–3.diff: The Gospels describe a possessed man who was blind and dumb (Luke, dumb), whereas The Urantia Book says it was a youth with a rebellious spirit and that this was the first case of actual demon possession.
acts.note.153:5.desc: Back at Bethsaida Jesus ate nothing and stayed alone in an upper room, and Joab reported that about one third of the evangelists had deserted. After midnight Jesus asked about thirty followers whether they too would go away, and Peter said the Master had taught the words of eternal life and they would never leave him.
acts.note.154:0.desc: On Saturday night, April 30, at Tiberias, commissioners of the Sanhedrin pressed Herod Antipas to arrest Jesus. Herod refused, trusting Chuza's report and harboring a superstitious fear over John the Baptist, and when they threatened to report him to Caesar, he ordered them out of his council chamber.
acts.note.154:1.desc: From May 1 to May 7 Jesus held counsel morning, afternoon, and evening at the Zebedee house with about one hundred tried disciples. On Friday the Capernaum synagogue was closed to Jesus and his followers, and Jairus resigned as chief ruler; fewer than one hundred fifty attended the last seaside meeting on May 7.
acts.note.154:2.desc: On May 8 the Sanhedrin decreed all the synagogues of Palestine closed to Jesus and his followers, and only the Hebron synagogue refused. Jesus declared a week's holiday and went fishing with David Zebedee, and he personally nursed Nathaniel and James Zebedee through a painful digestive illness without a miracle.
acts.note.154:3.desc: At the second Tiberias conference on May 16, Herod again refused to arrest Jesus, but on May 18 he agreed to the Sanhedrin's plan, provided the Roman rulers consented. When word of their consent came on the night of May 21, Herod signed the decree authorizing Jesus' arrest just before midnight.
acts.note.154:4.desc: That same Saturday night fifty leading citizens of Capernaum met at the synagogue and debated until after midnight what to do with Jesus. Apart from a few, they divided into four groups, regarding him as a harmless fanatic, a dangerous agitator, one in league with devils, or a man who was mad.
acts.note.154:5.desc: Before daybreak on Sunday, May 22, one of David's messengers brought word that Herod had authorized Jesus' arrest, and David called an emergency meeting for seven o'clock. Jesus gave his disciples farewell instructions, decided to take the twelve apostles and twelve evangelists with him, and about 7:30 began his parting address to almost one hundred believers.
acts.note.154:6.desc: About eight o'clock Mary, with James, Joseph, Jude, and Ruth, came to the Zebedee house to take Jesus home. When the message was passed in, Jesus said that those who do the will of his Father are his mother and brothers, and Mary collapsed. With word that the arresting officers were coming, Jesus had to leave without seeing his family.
acts.note.154:6.diff: The Gospels tell this briefly, whereas The Urantia Book adds that the Pharisees had stirred up the family, that Mary collapsed at his words, and that Jesus meant to see them but hasty flight prevented it.
acts.note.154:7.desc: About half past eight on the morning of May 22, Jesus fled by boat with the twelve apostles and twelve evangelists to the eastern side of the Sea of Galilee, followed by six of David's messengers. Leaving the boat near Kheresa, they began the wanderings of his last year, heading by way of Caesarea-Philippi toward the coast of Phoenicia.
acts.note.155:0.desc: After landing near Kheresa on Sunday, May 22, Jesus and the twenty-four went a little to the north and spent the night in a familiar park south of Bethsaida-Julias. Before retiring, the Master discussed with them the plan to go through Batanea and northern Galilee to the Phoenician coast.
acts.note.155:1.desc: That night Jesus quoted the Psalm asking why the heathen rage, but corrected its images of wrath and a rod of iron as unfit for his kingdom. The heathen concentrate their energies on their goals while the disciples hesitate, he said, and urged them to stop vain longings and build the kingdom through lives co-ordinated by truth.
acts.note.155:2.desc: On Monday, May 23, Peter went with the twelve evangelists to Chorazin, where they preached for two weeks but won few converts, a baptism of adversity. Jesus went with the eleven to Caesarea-Philippi, and when Peter's group joined them on June 8, he used the parable of the sower to teach the meaning of apparent failure.
acts.note.155:3.desc: During two weeks near Caesarea-Philippi Jesus did no public work but talked daily with the apostles. He taught that truth crystallized into a creed loses its life, that true religion is loyalty to one's highest convictions, and warned of the danger of accepting symbols and ceremonies in place of religious experience.
acts.note.155:3.diff: The Gospels place Peter's confession and the sayings on the church and the keys at Caesarea-Philippi, whereas in The Urantia Book this sojourn contains only quiet talks and teaching; Peter's confession comes later (157:3).
acts.note.155:4.desc: On Thursday, June 9, the twenty-five left Caesarea-Philippi and, going by way of Luz, reached Sidon on Friday afternoon. As they lunched in the shade of a rock ledge near Luz, Peter asked why they fled from their enemies, and Thomas asked how their religion differed from that of their enemies at Jerusalem.
acts.note.155:5.desc: After lunch Jesus distinguished primitive religion, the religion of fear; the religion of the mind, resting on traditional authority; and the religion of the spirit, based on personal experience. Unlike the religion of authority of the Jerusalem leaders, the religion of the spirit demands effort and the adventure of faith, and he sent the twenty-four to find their answer alone with the Father.
acts.note.155:6.desc: About three o'clock, in the shade of a hillside, Jesus at Peter's request taught more about the religion of the spirit. Religions of authority divide men, but the religion of the spirit unites them in experience amid diversity of belief; the proofs of knowing God are the fruits of the spirit in daily life and a life risked wholly on survival.
acts.note.156:0.desc: On Friday afternoon, June 10, Jesus and his party reached the environs of Sidon and stayed at the home of a well-to-do woman who had been a patient in the Bethsaida hospital. They spent about two and a half weeks in the Sidon region, and on the quiet Sabbath they meditated on the discourses on religion heard on the way.
acts.note.156:1.desc: On the Sabbath afternoon Norana, a Syrian woman, brought her twelve-year-old daughter, afflicted with a grievous nervous disorder with convulsions, to the home of Karuska. Peter and Thomas tried to send her away, and when Simon Zelotes said the children's bread should not be cast to the dogs, she persisted, speaking of the crumbs. Jesus came out, praised her faith, and healed the girl.
acts.note.156:1.diff: The Gospels have Jesus himself say the children's bread should not be given to dogs, whereas The Urantia Book gives the remark to Simon Zelotes, with Jesus overhearing through a window, and describes a nervous disorder.
acts.note.156:2.desc: Entering Sidon, Jesus said this world is only a bridge on which one should not build a dwelling. Staying at the home of Justa, he taught the twenty-four each morning, and they preached in Sidon afternoons and evenings, winning many gentiles. He taught spiritual progression and enjoyed the gentiles' keen sense of humor.
acts.map28.head: From Sidon along the Coast, and to Magadan Park
acts.map28.1.head: From Sidon to Porphyreon and Heldua
acts.map28.1.body: On Tuesday, June 28, they left Sidon, going up the coast. For a week the apostles preached in Porphyreon and the evangelists taught in Heldua.
acts.map28.2.head: Jesus alone at Beirut
acts.map28.2.body: Meanwhile, for three or four days, Jesus visited the coast city of Beirut, where he visited with a Syrian named Malach.
acts.map28.3.head: Back to Sidon, then to Tyre
acts.map28.3.body: On Wednesday, July 6, they all returned to Sidon and tarried at the home of Justa (dashed). On Sunday morning they went south by way of Sarepta, arriving at Tyre on Monday, July 11, and taught there until July 24. Jesus kept his headquarters at the home of Joseph, south of Tyre.
acts.map28.4.head: Ptolemais, Jotapata, Ramah, and Zebulun
acts.map28.4.body: About noon on Sunday, July 24, they left the home of Joseph and tarried a day at Ptolemais. On Tuesday they went inland by the Tiberias road to near Jotapata; on Thursday, by the Nazareth-Mount Lebanon trail, to Ramah, where they remained over the Sabbath, and reached Zebulun on Sunday, the 31st.
acts.map28.5.head: Near Gischala, then to Gennesaret
acts.map28.5.body: Leaving Zebulun, they journeyed to the junction with the Magdala-Sidon road near Gischala, and thence to Gennesaret, on the western shore south of Capernaum, to meet David Zebedee.
acts.map28.6.head: By Kheresa to Magadan Park
acts.map28.6.body: That very evening a boat took them across to near Kheresa. After a day of rest in the hills, they went on to the park where the five thousand had been fed and held conferences there for three days.
acts.note.156:3.desc: On June 28 the party left Sidon and taught for a week along the coast in Porphyreon and Heldua, while Jesus went to Beirut to visit a Syrian named Malach. Returning to Sidon on July 6, they went by way of Sarepta and reached Tyre on July 11.
acts.note.156:4.desc: From July 11 to 24 the apostles and evangelists taught two and two in Tyre and its environs, while Jesus made his headquarters at the home of Joseph south of the city. When Jesus spoke once, on the afternoon of July 20, the temple of Melkarth was opened to him, and many leaders in the making of Tyrian purple believed.
acts.note.156:5.desc: At Tyre Jesus taught the foundations of spiritual character through the story of the white lily and his first and only parable about carpentry. When Nathaniel asked about praying not to be led into temptation, he answered that temptation comes not from God but from selfishness and must be overcome by new spiritual affection. Before leaving he sent the twelve evangelists home by another route.
acts.note.156:6.desc: On July 24 Jesus and the twelve traveled by way of Ptolemais, Jotapata, Ramah, and Zebulun to Gennesaret, where they met David Zebedee, then conferred near Kheresa with about fifty remaining leaders. Opposition had subsided, and Philip and Herod Antipas sent word that they would not interfere with Jesus outside Galilee.
acts.map29.head: The Transfiguration on Mount Hermon and the Decapolis Tour
acts.map29.1.head: Over to Capernaum
acts.map29.1.body: On Sunday, August 7, Jesus went over with Andrew and Peter to meet his family, but the meeting did not take place. The temple tax was paid, and when it grew dark they rowed back toward the eastern shore (dashed).
acts.map29.2.head: To Caesarea-Philippi
acts.map29.2.body: On Monday, August 8, a conference at the park; early Tuesday morning they left. Passing south of the Waters of Merom, Jesus asked, "Who do men say that I am?" Late that evening they reached the home of Celsus.
acts.map29.3.head: The transfiguration on Mount Hermon
acts.map29.3.body: Near sundown on Friday, August 12, they reached the foot of Mount Hermon. On Monday, August 15, Jesus and three apostles began the ascent. On Tuesday morning they came down to the camp; the afflicted lad was healed, and they remained overnight with Celsus (dashed).
acts.map29.4.head: By Capernaum to Magadan Park
acts.map29.4.body: Leaving early Wednesday morning, just beyond the Waters of Merom they took the Damascus road to Capernaum. At twilight they went to the home of Simon Peter, and then crossed the lake to Magadan Park.
acts.map29.5.head: The tour of the Decapolis
acts.map29.5.body: On Thursday, August 18, twelve groups went out to labor in Gerasa, Gamala, Hippos, Zaphon, Gadara, Abila, Edrei, Philadelphia, Heshbon, Dium, Scythopolis, and other cities. Jesus visited the groups at Hippos, Gamala, Edrei, Abila, and Philadelphia (the roads are not in the text; dashed). On Friday, September 16, all assembled again at Magadan Park.
acts.note.157:0.desc: Jesus arranged to meet his whole Nazareth family on Sunday, August 7, at the Zebedee boatshop in Capernaum. But Pharisees from Jerusalem were encamped on the doorstep of Mary's house, watching it, so the family could not come out, Jesus gave up the visit, and once again they failed to meet.
acts.note.157:1.desc: By the lake near the boatshop a temple-tax collector asked Peter whether Jesus paid the temple tax, and Peter hastily promised he did. Having no money, Jesus told him to catch fish and sell them to pay the tax for the three of them, and a messenger of David and his fisherman friend handed Peter baskets of fish, so the tax was paid.
acts.note.157:1.diff: Matthew records a miracle of a shekel found in a fish's mouth, whereas The Urantia Book says the tax was paid from the sale of fish with the messenger's help, and the shekel story grew from Jesus' half-humorous remark.
acts.note.157:2.desc: On Monday, August 8, more than one hundred believers, evangelists, the women's corps, and Pharisees gathered at Magadan Park near Bethsaida-Julias. After rebuffing a demand for a sign at the public gathering, Jesus held an evening conference that decided on a united mission to the Decapolis, and he warned them to beware the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
acts.note.157:2.diff: The Gospels give the warning about leaven in a conversation in the boat with disciples who forgot bread, whereas The Urantia Book presents it as a long admonition at the close of the evening conference, with no mention of bread.
acts.sub.157:2.1–2: Pharisees ask for a sign of authority
acts.note.sub:157:2.1–2.desc: At the public meeting before the private conference, Pharisees heckled and disrupted the gathering, and their leader demanded a sign of Jesus' authority to teach. Jesus answered that they could discern the face of the sky but not the signs of the times, and that no sign would be given to a hypocritical generation.
acts.note.sub:157:2.1–2.diff: Matthew says no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah, whereas The Urantia Book does not mention Jonah and adds that a sign has already been given to those who would know the truth.
acts.note.157:3.desc: On Tuesday, on the way to Caesarea-Philippi, Jesus and the twelve sat under mulberry trees at lunch, and he asked for the first time, "Who do men say that I am?" When he asked who they said he was, Simon Peter exclaimed that he was the Deliverer, the Son of the living God, and the other eleven rose in agreement.
acts.note.157:3.diff: The Gospels set this in the region of Caesarea Philippi, whereas The Urantia Book places it at lunch on the way there, has Peter say "Deliverer" rather than "Christ," and says the eleven rose to join the confession.
acts.note.157:4.desc: At noon on Wednesday in the garden of Celsus, Jesus asked whether the apostles still held to Peter's declaration, and Peter again affirmed that he was the Son of God. Jesus said this confession was a revelation of his Father's spirit and that on this rock he would build the spiritual brotherhood, and he gave the apostles the keys of the outward kingdom.
acts.note.157:4.diff: Matthew says Jesus gave Peter personally the rock and the keys of the kingdom to build the church, whereas The Urantia Book says that the next day he founded the spiritual brotherhood on the twelve's confession, the keys meaning authority over social and economic matters.
acts.note.157:5.desc: What was new in Peter's confession was the clear recognition of Jesus' divinity as the Son of God. Since the Jewish concept of the Messiah held no divinity, Jesus gave up trying to modify that concept and chose to reveal his divinity, building the kingdom on the combined nature of the Son of Man and the Son of God.
acts.note.157:6.desc: Jesus and the apostles stayed another day at the home of Celsus, and that evening David Zebedee's messengers arrived with funds. With Peter's confession Jesus entered the fourth and last stage of his earth life, and in the garden he made new declarations about the obligations of sonship, his oneness with the Father, and his coming departure.
acts.note.157:7.desc: That evening Andrew talked privately with every apostle except Judas Iscariot, and troubled by Judas's attitude, he told Jesus late that night. Jesus told him to keep trusting Judas and to say nothing to anyone. On Friday morning, August 12, Jesus told the apostles to prepare to go to Mount Hermon.
acts.note.158:0.desc: Near sundown on Friday, August 12, A.D. 29, Jesus and the apostles reached the foot of Mount Hermon and spent two days in spiritual preparation. Jesus wished all the apostles to share the experience on the mountain, but since they could not attain that level, he chose to take only Peter, James, and John, who usually accompanied him on night vigils.
acts.note.158:1.desc: On Monday, August 15, Jesus climbed Mount Hermon with the three apostles and in the afternoon went apart alone to meet Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek. Awakened at night, the apostles saw the shining Jesus talking with two brilliant beings, and as Peter proposed building three tents, a silvery cloud overshadowed them and a voice said, "This is my beloved Son."
acts.note.158:1.diff: The Gospels say Moses and Elijah appeared, whereas The Urantia Book says the beings were actually Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek, and that Peter mistakenly supposed them to be Moses and Elijah.
acts.note.158:2.desc: Coming down the mountain, Jesus charged them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. Peter changed the subject by asking whether Elijah must first come, and Jesus answered that Elijah had already come but was not received; the three understood he meant John the Baptist.
acts.note.158:2.diff: The Gospels say the disciples simply asked about Elijah, whereas The Urantia Book explains that Peter asked it to divert the conversation away from Jesus' death and resurrection.
acts.note.158:3.desc: At the transfiguration the Eternal Son, through Gabriel, accepted the fullness of Michael's bestowal, and the Infinite Spirit, through the Father Melchizedek, testified to its satisfaction. The Father did not indicate the bestowal was finished but only bore witness through the Adjuster, "This is my beloved Son," and Jesus decided to pursue the mortal bestowal to its natural end.
acts.note.158:4.desc: On Tuesday morning Jesus reached the camp to find the nine apostles, Jerusalem scribes, and about fifty others in dispute. The day before, James of Safed had brought his only son, about fourteen, afflicted with epilepsy and possessed by a wandering midwayer; Simon Zelotes and then Andrew had tried to cast out the spirit and failed, while the scribes mocked them.
acts.note.158:4.diff: The Gospels say only that the disciples could not heal the boy, whereas The Urantia Book specifies that the apostles had been disputing who would be greatest, and that Simon Zelotes tried in Jesus' name, then Andrew, and both failed.
acts.note.158:5.desc: When Jesus returned, James of Safed knelt and begged him to heal his son. Jesus rebuked the faithless generation and said all things are possible to him who truly believes, and when the father asked help for his unbelief, Jesus took the lad by the hand and cast out the spirit, curing both the epilepsy and the possession.
acts.note.158:5.diff: The Gospels present it only as casting out a demon, whereas The Urantia Book calls it a double healing of physical epilepsy and a spirit malady from midwayer possession, with no saying about mustard-seed faith or prayer.
acts.note.158:6.desc: That evening at the home of Celsus, Thomas asked Jesus to explain the apostles' defeat. Jesus pointed out that they had yielded to the temptation of seeking high positions in a material kingdom, so their motives and ideals were not spiritual, and he declared that the Son of Man would be put to death but would rise again.
acts.note.158:7.desc: On Wednesday Jesus and the twelve left Caesarea-Philippi and traveled through Galilee by the Damascus road toward Capernaum. When Andrew asked about his sayings on death, Jesus revealed that he would be rejected and killed at Jerusalem and rise again; he rebuked Peter, who protested, saying "Get you behind me," and taught that whoever loses his life will save it.
acts.note.158:7.diff: The Gospels have Jesus call Peter Satan and bid them take up the cross, whereas in The Urantia Book he says they all savor of the spirit of the adversary and bids them take up their responsibilities daily; it occurs on the road back from Caesarea-Philippi.
acts.note.158:8.desc: At twilight in Simon Peter's home in Capernaum, Jesus asked what they had discussed on the way, and the apostles, who had been debating who would be greatest, held their peace. Setting one of Peter's little ones among them, Jesus taught that whoever humbles himself like this child is greatest, then they sailed across to Magadan.
acts.note.158:8.diff: Matthew says the disciples first asked who is greatest, whereas The Urantia Book, like Mark, has Jesus ask first, makes the child one of Peter's, and speaks of being shut out of the kingdom rather than hell fire.
acts.sub.158:8.1: Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble
acts.note.sub:158:8.1.desc: In the same place Jesus warned that whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble would be better off cast into the sea with a millstone about his neck. If the hands or eyes give offense in the progress of the kingdom, one should sacrifice those cherished idols, and the angels of the little ones always behold the faces of the heavenly hosts.
acts.note.sub:158:8.1.diff: Luke places this warning to the disciples on another occasion, whereas The Urantia Book gives it as part of the teaching with the child in Peter's home at Capernaum.
acts.intro.159: Setting out on the Decapolis tour
acts.note.159:0.desc: At Magadan Park almost one hundred evangelists and disciples, including the women's corps, were waiting. On Thursday, August 18, Jesus paired each apostle with an evangelist and sent them out in twelve groups to work for four weeks in the cities of the Decapolis, such as Gerasa, Gamala, and Hippos, to return by September 16.
acts.note.159:0.diff: Mark says only that Jesus passed through the Decapolis, whereas The Urantia Book describes an organized four-week mission by twelve groups in many cities, during which no miracles were performed.
acts.note.159:1.desc: One evening at Hippos, answering a disciple's question, Jesus taught about forgiveness. Because the Father goes out to seek sinners even before they think of repenting, his children should forgive one another; when Peter asked how often to forgive, Jesus answered with the parable of the steward who, forgiven his debt, imprisoned his fellow.
acts.note.159:1.diff: Matthew sets this teaching in a conversation with the disciples in the Capernaum period, whereas The Urantia Book places it in an evening discourse at Hippos during the Decapolis mission.
acts.sub.159:1.2: The hundred sheep and the one that strays
acts.note.sub:159:1.2.desc: Jesus spoke of the shepherd who leaves the ninety and nine to seek the lost sheep until he finds it and carries it home rejoicing, saying there is more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner. In the gospel of the kingdom, he taught, the Father goes out to look for sinners even before they think of repentance.
acts.note.sub:159:1.2.diff: Not found in the Bible, The Urantia Book adds that God does not merely receive the repentant but goes out to seek them before they even think of repenting.
acts.sub.159:1.3: If your brother sins against you
acts.note.sub:159:1.3.desc: Jesus said that if a brother sins, first go to him alone, then with one or two friends, and if he still will not hear, tell the brotherhood so it may act. The brotherhood cannot judge souls or forgive sins, but it may decide matters of temporal order and discipline, and he would be present wherever two or three believers are gathered.
acts.note.sub:159:1.3.diff: Matthew extends the church's power to bind and loose to whatever it decides, whereas The Urantia Book makes clear it excludes judging souls and forgiving sins and is limited to the brotherhood's temporal discipline.
acts.sub.159:1.4–5: The steward who owed a hundred denarii
acts.note.sub:159:1.4–5.desc: Simon Peter, in charge of the workers at Hippos, asked whether to forgive seven times, and Jesus answered, seventy times and seven. In the parable a chief steward forgiven ten thousand talents jailed a fellow steward who owed him a hundred denarii, so the king delivered him to the jailers; Jesus taught that mercy should be freely given.
acts.note.sub:159:1.4–5.diff: The parable's plot is the same, but Matthew ends with a warning that the Father will do likewise to the unforgiving, whereas The Urantia Book ends by saying more abundant mercy awaits those who show mercy.
acts.note.159:2.desc: Jesus went to Gamala to visit John and his associates. When John said he had forbidden a man at Ashtaroth to teach and cast out devils in Jesus' name, Jesus told him not to forbid him, for he who is not against us is for us. That man, Aden, went on working and raised up many believers at Kanata.
acts.note.159:2.diff: The Gospels tell briefly of an unnamed man, whereas The Urantia Book adds that he was Aden, who believed through the testimony of the Kheresa lunatic, ignored the prohibition, and gathered believers at Kanata.
acts.note.159:3.desc: At Edrei Jesus spent a day and a night with Thomas and his associates, teaching the principles for those who preach truth. They must respect personality and self-respect, never frighten people into the kingdom or rely on emotional appeals, not mistake strong feelings for the spirit's leading, and know that believers are not spared trouble but will pass through it with him.
acts.note.159:4.desc: At Abila, when Nathaniel asked privately about the truth of the Scriptures, Jesus answered him apart. The Scriptures are the work of men and faulty, yet the best collection of religious wisdom, and records such as a command to slay all enemies are not the word of God. Only the Creators possess infallibility, and the authority of truth is the living spirit.
acts.note.159:5.desc: At Philadelphia, when James asked how to choose the better passages of Scripture, Jesus gave several examples. He put the spirit of positive action into the passive doctrines of the Jewish religion, teaching that turning the other cheek and going the second mile are positive acts of overcoming evil with good.
acts.note.159:6.desc: The four-week Decapolis mission was moderately successful, and hundreds were received into the kingdom. On Friday, September 16, the whole corps assembled at Magadan Park, and on the Sabbath more than one hundred believers held a council. Abner moved his base to Bethlehem, and Jesus and his associates prepared for a last week of rest.
acts.note.160:0.desc: On Sunday, September 18, Andrew announced that no work was planned for the week, and all the apostles except Nathaniel and Thomas went home. Jesus rested almost completely, leaving Nathaniel and Thomas to discuss with Rodan, a Greek philosopher from Alexandria who had come to Magadan, hearing him and teaching him the gospel.
acts.note.160:1.desc: From Monday Rodan gave ten addresses to Nathaniel, Thomas, and about two dozen believers. Human life consists of urges, desires, and lures, he said, and maturity lies in converting them into higher ideals; the greatest method of problem solving he had learned from Jesus is the isolation of worshipful meditation.
acts.note.160:2.desc: Rodan taught that humans build personality and culture by communicating meanings and values through symbols. Associations of friendship and mutual affection, above all marriage, are central to the art of living, fostering self-expression and understanding, union of souls, enthusiasm for living, and defense against evil.
acts.note.160:3.desc: Rodan said the energy needed for maturity comes not from emotional excitement but from worship, which unites meditation and relaxation in spiritual communion. When such practice becomes habit it forms spiritual character, and the Master's way of finding the key to a locked door through tact and tolerance is better than fighting.
acts.note.160:4.desc: Rodan said that while seeking eternal realities one must provide for the necessities of temporal life: health, clear thinking, ability and skill, wealth, the ability to withstand defeat, and culture. One must learn to fail gracefully, and for the God-seeking man failure is simply an educational episode in acquiring wisdom.
acts.note.160:5.desc: Rodan defined religion as the experience of reacting to what is worthy of the devotion of all mankind, holding that true religion rests on spirit experience and cannot exist without the supreme ideal of the eternal God. Professing Jesus' religion as the highest concept of religion, he declared that he too had embarked on this eternal adventure.
acts.map30.head: Headquarters Moved to Pella, and Visits to Jerusalem
acts.map30.1.head: Up to Jerusalem for the feast of tabernacles
acts.map30.1.body: Announced on Sunday, September 25; they started early the next day. They passed down the eastern shore of the lake and by way of Scythopolis entered the borders of Samaria. Refused lodging at a village on the eastern slopes of Mount Gilboa, they stopped for the night at the village near the Jordan ford. Early the next day they crossed the river and went by the east Jordan highway, arriving at Bethany late Wednesday evening.
acts.map30.2.head: Teaching in the temple; Abner at Bethlehem
acts.map30.2.body: During the feast Jesus publicly taught in the temple on several occasions. He divided his time about equally between Bethany and Bethlehem, where Abner was making his headquarters.
acts.map30.3.head: From Ephraim to Magadan Park
acts.map30.3.body: In the latter part of October they withdrew from near Jerusalem and rested a few days at Ephraim. Leaving on Sunday, October 30, by the west Jordan highway, they arrived late on Wednesday, November 2. On November 19 the seventy were ordained.
acts.map30.4.head: Headquarters moved to the Pella camp
acts.map30.4.body: On Tuesday, December 6, almost three hundred started out at daybreak to lodge that night near Pella by the river, by the spring where John the Baptist had once camped (the route is not in the text; dashed).
acts.map30.5.head: In secret to Jerusalem for the feast of dedication
acts.map30.5.body: With Nathaniel and Thomas, Jesus crossed the Jordan at the Bethany ford and lodged at Jericho. On Friday night he met with leaders at the home of Nicodemus; on Sabbath morning, after breakfast at Bethany, he healed Josiah, born blind, near the temple. With Josiah he went back to Pella.
acts.note.161:0.desc: On Sunday, September 25, A.D. 29, at Magadan, Jesus announced that the next day he and the twelve apostles would leave for Jerusalem to attend the feast of tabernacles. He directed the evangelists to visit the believers in Galilee and the women's corps to return to Bethsaida, while Nathaniel and Thomas stayed some days at Magadan to continue their discussions with Rodan.
acts.note.161:1.desc: Rodan contended that personality requires communication between equals, so God, having no equal, cannot be a person. By Tuesday night Nathaniel won him over with arguments such as the Father's communication with the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit and Jesus' communication with both the Father and men, and Rodan confessed God as a person.
acts.note.161:2.desc: Nathaniel and Thomas explained to Rodan the divine nature of Jesus. Pointing to his flawless friendship and sinless life, perfect emotional control, superhuman knowledge, authority as a divine teacher, claim to be one with the Father, and prayer as if face to face, they said he was both Son of Man and Son of God. Rodan later gave his life in Greece.
acts.note.161:3.desc: Jesus' consciousness of divinity grew gradually up to his baptism, after which he seems to have been able to choose whether to rely only on his human mind or also to use the knowledge of the divine mind. He often concealed his foreknowledge and thought discernment from his associates, and the recorders cannot fully distinguish these two techniques or the whole mystery.
acts.intro.162: James and John would call down fire
acts.note.162:0.desc: Jesus and the ten apostles planned to go to Jerusalem through Samaria, but a village on the eastern slopes of Mount Gilboa refused them lodging because they were Jews and drove out Philip and Matthew. When James and John asked to call down fire from heaven, Jesus sternly rebuked them; they lodged at a village by the Jordan ford and reached Bethany on Wednesday.
acts.note.162:0.diff: The Gospel of Luke says only that messengers were sent ahead, whereas The Urantia Book specifies that Philip and Matthew indignantly spoke of the Holy One of Israel and were chased out with sticks and stones.
acts.note.162:1.desc: At the sudden decision to attend the feast of tabernacles at Jerusalem, the apostles feared for his life, but Jesus answered that the hour had now come. Thanks to division within the Sanhedrin, the efforts of Abner's associates, and his own boldness, he was able to teach publicly in the temple courts, an open proclamation of his divinity.
acts.note.162:2.desc: On the first afternoon Jesus taught in the temple, asked how he could teach without studying under the rabbis, he answered that his teaching was that of Him who sent him. He also answered why the rulers sought to kill him and whether he was the Messiah, and Eber, the Sanhedrin officer sent to arrest him, was so moved that he refused to do so.
acts.note.162:2.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus went up secretly after his brothers urged him, whereas The Urantia Book says he went with the apostles, names the officer who came to arrest him and returned as Eber, and records his protest.
acts.note.162:3.desc: On the third morning of the feast, agents of the Sanhedrin dragged before Jesus a woman said to be taken in adultery, to entrap him. Jesus wrote three times in the sand, causing her husband, the accusers, and her partner in sin to depart in turn, and said, "Neither do I condemn you." The woman, Hildana, forsook her husband and joined the disciples.
acts.note.162:3.diff: The Gospel of John says scribes and Pharisees brought her and Jesus said whoever is without sin should cast the first stone, whereas The Urantia Book says it was a trap arranged with her husband and Jesus scattered them by writing in the sand.
acts.note.162:4.desc: The feast of tabernacles, drawing people from Spain to India, was an ideal occasion for Jesus to proclaim his full gospel publicly in Jerusalem. The feast is described: the sacrifice of seventy bullocks, the pouring of water drawn from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher with wine upon the altar, and Psalms chanted while waving branches.
acts.note.162:5.desc: On the evening of the next to the last day of the feast, in the temple courts lit by candelabras and torches, Jesus declared, "I am the light of the world." He said he and the Father bear witness together, that he is from above, and that when the Son of Man is lifted up all will know; many believed, and no one dared lay hands on him.
acts.note.162:5.diff: The Gospel of John places these words at the treasury, whereas The Urantia Book makes them a discourse to the throng on the evening before the last day of the feast, under the light of candelabras and torches.
acts.note.162:6.desc: On the last great day of the feast, just after the water and wine were poured on the altar and the Hallel was chanted, Jesus cried out, "If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink." He said that after the Son of Man finished his work, the Spirit of Truth would be poured out upon all flesh, and the crowd was divided about him.
acts.note.162:6.diff: In the Gospel of John the writer comments that the Spirit was not yet given, whereas in The Urantia Book Jesus himself says the Spirit of Truth will be poured out upon all flesh after he finishes his work.
acts.note.162:7.desc: On the afternoon of the last day, Jesus taught the believers in Solomon's Porch that the truth shall make them free, speaking of the freedom of the soul and sonship. When opponents shouted that he was a child of the devil, he said, "Before Abraham was, I am," and departed, escaping to a secret place near Bethany while they went for stones.
acts.note.162:7.diff: The Gospel of John has Jesus flatly say their father is the devil, whereas in The Urantia Book he asks whether they have chosen to be children of evil, and he withdraws to where Martha, Mary, and Lazarus awaited him.
acts.note.162:8.desc: Avoiding arrest, Jesus lodged with Lazarus and his sisters at a friend's house. While Lazarus and Mary sat at Jesus' feet listening, Martha, preparing the meal, asked him to bid Mary help her; Jesus answered that Mary had chosen the good part and told them to learn to serve together.
acts.note.162:8.diff: The Gospel of Luke sets this in an unnamed village, whereas The Urantia Book places it near Bethany with Lazarus and his sisters and adds that Jesus told them to work and serve together.
acts.note.162:9.desc: After the feast of tabernacles Jesus did not teach again in the temple but went between Bethany and Bethlehem, instructing Abner and John's former apostles until they fully believed. Abner and his eleven fellows agreed to join him in early November, and on October 30 Jesus' party left Ephraim, reaching Magadan Park on November 2.
acts.note.163:0.desc: A few days after Jesus and the twelve returned to Magadan, Abner and about fifty disciples arrived from Bethlehem. From November 4 to 19 Jesus intensively trained about one hundred fifty tried disciples; Peter taught public preaching, Nathaniel the art of teaching, Thomas how to answer questions, and Matthew directed group finances.
acts.note.163:1.desc: On Sabbath afternoon, November 19, at the Magadan Camp, before more than four hundred believers, Jesus ordained the seventy and placed Abner at their head. He sent them two and two as lambs among wolves, without purse, to bring peace and minister to the sick, and they went through Galilee, Samaria, and Judea for about six weeks.
acts.note.163:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke has them shake the dust from their feet against unreceptive towns, which will fare worse than Sodom, whereas The Urantia Book omits this and tells them to proclaim, even in leaving, that the kingdom is at hand.
acts.note.163:2.desc: More than fifty candidates for the seventy were rejected, and those who wished first to bury a father or comfort their family withdrew after talking with Jesus. Matadormus, a rich young member of the Sanhedrin, was told that to become a messenger he must sell his goods and give to the poor, and he went away sorrowful, though he later became treasurer of the Jerusalem church.
acts.note.163:2.diff: The Gospels tell only of a rich young man asking about eternal life, whereas The Urantia Book says he was asked to give up his wealth because he sought to be one of the seventy, and that Jesus already recognized him as a disciple and son of the kingdom.
acts.note.163:3.desc: After Matadormus left, Jesus said it is hard for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom. When the apostles asked if all must give up their wealth, he said only those who would be apostles must, and that whoever has left all will receive many times more, telling the parable of the vineyard owner who paid a denarius even to the latest workers.
acts.note.163:3.diff: Matthew's promise that the twelve will sit on twelve thrones judging the tribes of Israel is absent in The Urantia Book, which makes clear that giving up property is required only of those who would live with the apostles.
acts.note.163:4.desc: On the morning the seventy departed, Jesus told them to preach the gospel to gentiles too, not to teach the expectation of miracles, to make clear that the time had come for an open break with the Jerusalem leaders, and to sum up all duty as love of God and neighbor. Then Simon Peter charged them to devotion, courage, faith, zeal, courtesy, and ministry to the sick.
acts.note.163:5.desc: After spending the last ten days of November in council at Magadan, almost three hundred people moved on Tuesday, December 6, to Perea near Pella, by the spring where John the Baptist had camped. David Zebedee curtailed the messenger service and on December 18 moved his equipment, preparing a camp north of the apostolic camp for fifteen hundred people.
acts.note.163:6.desc: On Friday, December 30, the seventy returned to Pella and reported their experiences. Jesus said he saw Satan fall as lightning, told them to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, and gave thanks to the Father. He pronounced woe on cities that had not received his messengers, and the next day warned the seventy against spiritual pride.
acts.note.163:6.diff: The power to tread on serpents and scorpions in Luke is absent in The Urantia Book, which says the subjection of devils mostly meant cures of nervous disorders and adds that after returning to the Father he would send his spirit, ending spirit possession.
acts.note.163:7.desc: At the Pella camp preparations were completed for the last mission, a three months' tour of all Perea. People came from the whole Roman world and the Near East, and Jesus spent much time teaching at Pella. The women's corps trained fifty new women, and Perpetua, Simon Peter's wife, took charge of the women's work under Abner.
acts.note.164:0.desc: While the Pella camp was being set up, Jesus took Nathaniel and Thomas and went secretly up to Jerusalem for the feast of the dedication. The two apostles earnestly protested that he was putting himself into the hands of the Sanhedrin, but Jesus answered that he would give the teachers of Israel another chance to see the light, and they lodged at Jericho.
acts.note.164:1.desc: That evening in Jericho a lawyer tried to entrap Jesus by asking about eternal life and who his neighbor was. Jesus told of a man fallen among robbers whom a priest and a Levite passed by but a Samaritan cared for, and the lawyer, avoiding the word Samaritan, answered, "He who showed mercy."
acts.note.164:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke gives no time or place, whereas The Urantia Book sets it at an evening gathering in Jericho on the way to the feast of dedication and explains that the lawyer avoided the odious word Samaritan.
acts.note.164:2.desc: Jesus went to the feast of the dedication to give the Sanhedrin and the Jewish leaders another chance to see the light. On Friday night about twenty-five believing leaders, including Eber, Matadormus, and Joseph of Arimathea, met at the home of Nicodemus, and Jesus amazed them with his learning but told them their plans would be of no avail.
acts.note.164:3.desc: On the Sabbath morning near the temple Jesus met Josiah, a beggar born blind. Asked by Nathaniel whose sin caused it, he said no one's; he anointed his eyes with clay mixed with spittle and had him wash in the pool of Siloam, and he saw. It was an open challenge to the Sanhedrin and a lesson not to despise material means of healing.
acts.note.164:3.diff: The Gospel of John presents it simply as a sign, whereas The Urantia Book explains that Josiah neither asked for healing nor had much faith, and that Jesus chose the Sabbath and used clay and spittle deliberately to challenge the Sanhedrin.
acts.note.164:4.desc: As Josiah's healing caused a stir, about fifty members of the Sanhedrin met, breaking their rule against Sabbath sessions, and questioned Josiah and his parents. Division arose among them, and Josiah declared that he was blind but now sees and that if this man were not from God he could do nothing; he was cast out of the synagogue.
acts.note.164:4.diff: The Gospel of John describes an interrogation by Pharisees, whereas The Urantia Book says it was a Sanhedrin session violating the Sabbath rule, and that Jesus intended this to bring the matter before the Sanhedrin.
acts.note.164:5.desc: While the Sanhedrin met, Jesus taught for more than two hours in Solomon's Porch in midwinter. Asked to say plainly if he was the Messiah, he answered that his sheep hear his voice and that he and the Father are one, and he narrowly escaped stoning. Afterward he sought out the outcast Josiah, confirmed his faith, and took him to Pella.
acts.note.164:5.diff: The Gospel of John's quotation "You are gods" is absent in The Urantia Book, which places the visit to the outcast Josiah's home after this teaching and says Jesus took him to the Pella camp.
acts.map31.head: The Perean Tour, and to Bethany to Raise Lazarus
acts.map31.1.head: The Pella camp and the Perean mission
acts.map31.1.body: On Tuesday, January 3, A.D. 30, Abner sent the seventy on a mission to all the cities and villages of Perea. For almost three months Jesus divided his time between the camp at Pella and trips with the twelve to the cities where the seventy taught.
acts.map31.2.head: Ragaba and Amathus
acts.map31.2.body: On Sabbath, February 18, at Ragaba, Jesus was the guest of honor at the breakfast of Nathaniel, a wealthy Pharisee. The next day, approaching Amathus, near the border of Samaria, he healed ten lepers.
acts.map31.3.head: To Abner at Philadelphia
acts.map31.3.body: By way of Gerasa they arrived at Philadelphia on Wednesday, February 22. Very late on Sunday night, February 26, came word from Bethany: "Lord, he whom you love is very sick."
acts.map31.4.head: To Bethany: Lazarus raised
acts.map31.4.body: After tarrying two full days, they set out early Wednesday morning and spent that night in Jericho. Shortly after noon on Thursday Jesus came near Bethany and raised Lazarus, who had been dead four days.
acts.map31.5.head: Back to the Pella camp
acts.map31.5.body: After resting over the Sabbath with friends in Bethpage, a hamlet near Bethany, they started early Sunday morning on the journey back to the Pella encampment (the route is not in the text; dashed).
acts.note.165:0.desc: On Tuesday, January 3, A.D. 30, Abner gave the seventy messengers their final instructions and sent them to all the cities and villages of Perea. This Perean mission lasted almost three months and was the Master's last ministry; Jesus stayed at the Pella camp or went about with the twelve to assist the seventy.
acts.note.165:1.desc: By the middle of January more than twelve hundred persons had gathered at Pella. Jesus usually taught the multitude at nine o'clock in the morning and reserved the evenings for question-and-answer sessions with the apostles. By the middle of March, when he set out for Jerusalem, over four thousand came each morning.
acts.note.165:2.desc: After the feast of the dedication, Pharisees and teachers who had followed him from Jerusalem to Pella heard Jesus preach on the Good Shepherd. He declared himself the door of the sheepfold and the true shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and has power to take it up again. The next day about half of these teachers professed belief.
acts.note.165:2.diff: The Gospel of John places this sermon in Jerusalem right after the healing of the blind man, whereas The Urantia Book sets it at Pella before Pharisees who followed him there, adding that his other sheep are not of this world only.
acts.note.165:3.desc: On Sabbath, January 28, Jesus preached to almost three thousand at Pella on Trust and Spiritual Preparedness. He warned against the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, told them not to fear those who can kill the body, and to trust a Father who values them above sparrows. Afterward many were baptized by the apostles in the Jordan.
acts.note.165:3.diff: The Gospels say to fear him who has power to cast into hell, whereas The Urantia Book says to fear no one and rejoice in knowing him who can save; it also softens the sin against the Holy Spirit to one rarely forgiven.
acts.note.165:4.desc: While the baptizing went on, a young man asked Jesus to make his brother divide their inheritance with him. Jesus refused to act as a divider and warned against covetousness. He taught that honest wealth is no sin but must never become master, and that the rich must answer three questions in the judgment.
acts.note.165:4.diff: The Gospel of Luke ends briefly with the refusal and the warning against covetousness, whereas The Urantia Book adds that the young man later came back privately and was advised to go to the synagogue court, and lists the three questions for the wealthy.
acts.sub.165:4.2–3: The story of the foolish rich man
acts.note.sub:165:4.2–3.desc: Jesus told of a rich man whose ground brought forth plentifully, who pulled down his barns to build greater ones and told his soul to take its ease. He had laid up no treasure in heaven; that very night robbers broke in, killed him, plundered and burned his barns, and his heirs fell to quarreling.
acts.note.sub:165:4.2–3.diff: The Gospel of Luke says God required the man's soul that night, whereas The Urantia Book says specifically that robbers broke in that night, killed him, burned his barns, and that his heirs fought over the estate.
acts.note.165:5.desc: That evening, at Andrew's request, Jesus spoke to the apostles alone about wealth and self-support. Those who had given their lives to the kingdom as ambassadors should consider the ravens and the lilies and not be anxious about food and clothing, but believing disciples must earn their own bread. He also urged them to watch like servants awaiting their lord's return from the wedding feast.
acts.note.165:5.diff: The Gospel of Luke continues these words to the disciples before the crowd, whereas The Urantia Book says they were spoken that evening to the apostles only, limiting freedom from anxiety to the apostles while ordinary disciples must earn their own living.
acts.note.165:6.desc: When Peter asked whether the parable was for the apostles, Jesus contrasted the tested and proved faithful steward with the idle servant, saying that much is required of those to whom much is given. He spoke of a baptism he must undergo and foretold that the gospel would divide families. The next day he went into northern Perea.
acts.note.165:6.diff: The Gospel of Luke's words about casting fire on the earth and servants beaten with many or few stripes are absent from The Urantia Book, which instead closes with a charge to proclaim the gospel to all the world and every nation.
acts.note.166:0.desc: From February 11 to 20, Jesus and the twelve toured the cities and villages of northern Perea where Abner's associates and the women's corps were working, and found them meeting with success. Jesus repeatedly pointed out that the gospel could spread without miracles, and from this time it reflected his teachings more than his person.
acts.note.166:1.desc: On Sabbath, February 18, Nathaniel, a wealthy Pharisee of Ragaba, invited Jesus to breakfast with about twenty Pharisees. When Jesus did not perform the ceremonial hand washing, they murmured. Jesus rebuked the hypocrisy of cleansing only the outside of the cup, the parading of tithes, and the lawyers' heavy burdens, and left without eating.
acts.note.166:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke sets this at an unnamed meal and Matthew makes it a sermon before the crowds in Jerusalem, whereas The Urantia Book places it at Nathaniel's breakfast in Ragaba and says Jesus left without eating.
acts.note.166:2.desc: The next day, near Amathus on the Samaritan border, Jesus met ten lepers, nine Jews and one Samaritan. Despite Simon Zelotes' wish to avoid the Samaritan, he sent them to show themselves to the priests, and all were healed on the way, but only the Samaritan returned to give thanks.
acts.note.166:2.diff: The Gospel of Luke calls all ten lepers, whereas The Urantia Book says only four had real leprosy and six had skin diseases. The exchange with Simon Zelotes is not in the Bible.
acts.note.166:3.desc: At Gerasa a believing Pharisee asked whether few or many would be saved. Jesus answered that salvation depends first on personal choice. The gate of life is narrow, yet broad enough for all who sincerely seek to enter, and he himself is that gate; he warned the selfish who delay until the door is shut.
acts.note.166:3.diff: The Gospel of Luke only urges striving to enter the narrow door, whereas The Urantia Book explains that the gate is wide enough for all who wish, that Jesus himself is the gate, and that the number saved depends on how many accept the invitation.
acts.note.166:4.desc: At a noon stop on the way to Philadelphia, Thomas asked whether spirit beings prevent accidents. Jesus said that seeing prosperity and adversity as acts of God is superstition. The Galileans killed by Pilate and the eighteen crushed by the tower of Siloam were innocent victims of the accidents of time, and he told the parable of the fig tree.
acts.note.166:4.diff: The Gospel of Luke warns that unless they repent all will likewise perish, whereas The Urantia Book calls the victims innocent casualties of accident and ends the fig tree story with an abundant harvest from obeying the laws of fruitfulness.
acts.note.166:5.desc: Jesus and the twelve visited Abner, who was teaching in Philadelphia. The Philadelphia synagogue, never under the Sanhedrin's supervision, later became the center of the eastern missionary church. Abner, estranged from James, Peter, and Paul, headed that church until he died at Philadelphia on November 21, A.D. 74, at the age of 89.
acts.note.167:0.desc: During the Perean ministry usually only ten apostles were with Jesus, since at least two were always left at Pella to teach the multitude. Jesus and the ten arrived at Philadelphia on Wednesday, February 22, rested Thursday and Friday, and on Friday night James spoke in the synagogue.
acts.note.167:1.desc: A wealthy Pharisee of Philadelphia who had accepted Abner's teachings invited Jesus and about forty leading men to a Sabbath breakfast. Jesus healed a believer suffering from dropsy on the Sabbath, taught the guests to take the lowest seats at a feast, and told the host to invite the poor who cannot repay him.
acts.note.167:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke speaks only of a ruler of the Pharisees, whereas The Urantia Book makes the host a believer in Abner's teachings at Philadelphia, says the sick man did not ask for healing, and mentions a Sanhedrist who missed the seat of honor.
acts.note.167:2.desc: At the same breakfast a lawyer remarked, 'Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.' Jesus told the parable of a ruler's great supper whose invited guests made excuses, so he filled his house with the poor and those from the highways. The next day the apostles debated its meaning, but Jesus told each to find his own interpretation.
acts.note.167:2.diff: This sequel is not in the Bible: The Urantia Book adds that one scoffing Pharisee was baptized that day, that Abner preached on the parable that night, and that Jesus declined to interpret it.
acts.note.167:3.desc: After the Sabbath synagogue service Abner had arranged, Jesus touched an elderly woman long bent in form through fear, and by faith she immediately straightened up. The unfriendly ruler of the synagogue who criticized the healing was put to shame and was later removed from office.
acts.note.167:3.diff: The Gospel of Luke says the woman had a spirit of infirmity and was bound by Satan, whereas The Urantia Book explains her affliction as wholly mental, born of fear, and adds that the ruler of the synagogue was later dismissed.
acts.note.167:4.desc: Late on Sunday night, February 26, a runner from Martha and Mary of Bethany reported that Lazarus was very sick. To give the Jerusalem leaders a last chance, Jesus waited two more days so the fourth day would pass, then proposed going into Judea. The apostles objected, but Thomas said, 'let us go also that we may die with him.'
acts.note.167:4.diff: The Gospel of John gives no reason for the two-day delay, whereas The Urantia Book cites the Jewish belief that the soul never lingered near the body after the third day, and names James as the one who objected.
acts.note.167:5.desc: Almost fifty followers went with Jesus toward Judea. At Wednesday's noon lunch he taught the terms of salvation and told the parable of the Pharisee and the publican. That night in Jericho the Pharisees tried to entrap him on divorce, but he avoided the dispute and taught the high ideals of marriage.
acts.sub.167:5.1: The parable of the Pharisee and the publican
acts.note.sub:167:5.1.desc: At Wednesday's noon lunch on the way to Bethany, Jesus taught that salvation is a free gift to all who have faith, and told the parable of the Pharisee who boasted of himself in the temple and the publican who beat his breast and asked for mercy. The publican went home approved of God.
acts.note.sub:167:5.1.diff: The Gospel of Luke gives only the parable, whereas The Urantia Book places it at the noon lunch on the way to Lazarus, as the close of a lesson on the terms of salvation.
acts.sub.167:5.2–8: Teaching on marriage and divorce at Jericho
acts.note.sub:167:5.2–8.desc: That night in Jericho hostile Pharisees tried to entrap Jesus with questions about marriage and divorce. He avoided debating the divorce laws, exalted marriage as the highest human relationship, and condemned the practice of putting away wives for trivial reasons as an injustice to women and children.
acts.note.sub:167:5.2–8.diff: The Gospels have Jesus declare that divorce and remarriage, except for unchastity, is adultery, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus refused to issue any new commands or pronouncements on divorce and only upheld the equality of women.
acts.note.167:6.desc: When his teaching on marriage and children spread through Jericho, scores of mothers brought their little ones the next morning for his blessing. The apostles tried to send them away, but Jesus, indignant, told them not to forbid the children and blessed them with his hands. He then taught the value of beauty and nature in children's worship.
acts.note.167:6.diff: The Gospels do not name the place, whereas The Urantia Book says it happened in Jericho before breakfast, and softens the saying so that those who do not receive the kingdom as a little child will hardly grow up to spiritual maturity.
acts.note.167:7.desc: On the hill road from Jericho to Bethany, Nathaniel asked what to teach about angels. Jesus explained that angels are a separate order of created beings, never mortals who have died, and that they link the worlds and guide souls after death. While he spoke, Martha came out to meet them.
acts.note.168:0.desc: Shortly after noon on Thursday, as Jesus came over the hill near Bethany, Martha went out to meet him. Lazarus had been dead four days and was laid in the family tomb at the far end of the garden on Sunday afternoon. Jesus told Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, and then Mary came and fell at his feet.
acts.note.168:0.diff: The Gospel of John says Martha went out on hearing Jesus was coming, whereas The Urantia Book says she had posted a lad to watch the road and went out alone to avoid trouble with enemies from Jerusalem, quietly sending for Mary.
acts.note.168:1.desc: Jesus asked where Lazarus had been laid and wept as he followed the sisters to the tomb, moved by sympathy for them, displeasure at the show of mourning, and hesitancy to call Lazarus back to a life of persecution. About half past two on Thursday afternoon he ordered the stone removed, and the apostles and neighbors rolled it away.
acts.note.168:1.diff: The Gospel of John gives no reason for his tears and distress, whereas The Urantia Book names three reasons and adds that fifteen minutes before Lazarus died his Thought Adjuster was ordered held in waiting.
acts.note.168:2.desc: As some forty-five people stood before the tomb, Jesus thanked the Father and cried, 'Lazarus, come forth!' The celestial hosts under Gabriel acted, and in twelve seconds Lazarus sat up. He had been conscious of nothing during the four days. Many believed, but the Sanhedrin was soon called together.
acts.note.168:2.diff: The Gospel of John says only that the dead man came out, whereas The Urantia Book says celestial hosts carried out the resurrection, Lazarus's Adjuster returned, and this was the only such restoration in the mortal body on Urantia.
acts.map32.head: From the Pella Camp to Jerusalem
acts.map32.1.head: From Bethany to the Pella camp
acts.map32.1.body: After the raising of Lazarus they left Bethany secretly early on Sunday morning and arrived at the Pella camp late on Monday evening, March 6. The route is not in the text (dashed).
acts.map32.2.head: From Pella to Heshbon
acts.map32.2.body: On Saturday, March 11, the last sermon at Pella. On Monday, March 13, they left the Pella encampment; at the Bethany ford of the Jordan, sometimes called Bethabara, Jesus delivered "Counting the Cost" and started off for Heshbon.
acts.map32.3.head: Tour of southern Perea
acts.map32.3.body: For more than two weeks they visited the towns where the seventy labored. At Heshbon Abner saw Jesus in the flesh for the last time. On Wednesday evening, March 29, they encamped at Livias.
acts.map32.4.head: By Jericho to Bethany
acts.map32.4.body: On March 30 Bartimeus was healed at Jericho, and Jesus abode at the house of Zaccheus. Leaving near noon on the 31st, they arrived at Bethany shortly after four o'clock.
acts.map32.5.head: Entry into Jerusalem, April 2 (inset)
acts.map32.5.body: Riding the colt of an ass brought from Bethpage, he went over the brow of Olivet to the temple, and in the evening went back to Bethany (dashed).
acts.note.168:3.desc: At one o'clock on Friday the Sanhedrin met. A resolution to put Jesus to death without trial was offered but never voted on, because fourteen members resigned. Although they heard the testimony of Lazarus and his sisters, they attributed the miracle to the prince of devils. Jesus spent the Sabbath at Bethpage and left for Pella on Sunday.
acts.note.168:3.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus withdrew to a town called Ephraim, whereas The Urantia Book says he spent the Sabbath at Bethpage and returned to Pella, and adds the fourteen resignations and the summoning of Lazarus.
acts.note.168:4.desc: On the way from Bethany to Pella the apostles asked about answers to prayer, since Lazarus had died even though the sickness was 'not to the death.' Jesus taught in ten points that a delayed answer may be a better one, and that every sincere, spirit-born petition is answered, though conditioned by time and space.
acts.note.168:5.desc: Lazarus stayed at Bethany until the days of the crucifixion, when he was warned that the Sanhedrin had decreed his death, and he fled across the Jordan to Abner at Philadelphia. Martha and Mary later joined him. Lazarus became treasurer of the church at Philadelphia and died at the age of 67.
acts.note.169:0.desc: Late on Monday evening, March 6, Jesus and the ten apostles returned to the Pella camp, which was already stirred by news of Lazarus's resurrection. During this last week there he preached to the crowds every afternoon. Meanwhile, the Pharisees and chief priests were formulating their charges against him.
acts.note.169:1.desc: On Thursday afternoon Jesus preached on the Grace of Salvation, retelling the stories of the lost sheep and the lost coin and adding his favorite parable of the prodigal son. The father ran out to welcome the son who had wasted his inheritance and reasoned with the angry elder brother. God accepts and seeks men even before they repent.
acts.note.169:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke does not describe the brothers' characters, whereas The Urantia Book portrays two brothers who always quarreled and has the father tell the elder son he could have had a kid any time had he cultivated friends.
acts.note.sub:169:1.2.desc: To show that God seeks man even as man seeks God, Jesus again told of the shepherd who left the ninety and nine in the fold to search for the one lost sheep and carried it home on his shoulder. A straying soul only increases the Father's interest.
acts.note.sub:169:1.2.diff: The Gospel of Luke presents it as a reply to the Pharisees' murmuring about receiving sinners, whereas The Urantia Book has it retold at Pella in the sermon on the grace of salvation, explaining that sheep go astray without intending to.
acts.note.sub:169:1.4.desc: Jesus told of the woman who had ten pieces of silver made into a necklace, lost one, lit a lamp, swept the house until she found it, and rejoiced with her neighbors. The Father and the Son use every influence to seek the lost, and the coin stands for those hidden by the dust of life.
acts.note.sub:169:1.4.diff: The Gospel of Luke mentions only ten coins, whereas The Urantia Book says they formed a necklace of adornment and explains the coin as those spiritually blinded by the material cares of life.
acts.note.169:2.desc: When Simon Zelotes asked why the children of the world are called wiser, Jesus told the parable of the shrewd steward who reduced his master's debtors' bills to prepare for his dismissal. He who is faithful in little is faithful in much, and no one can serve God and mammon. When the Pharisees scoffed, he withdrew to his tent.
acts.note.169:2.diff: The Gospel of Luke presents the parable as spoken to the disciples, whereas The Urantia Book makes it an answer to Simon Zelotes and adds that the steward had oppressed his master's clients and squandered his funds.
acts.note.169:3.desc: When the meeting grew noisy with the Pharisees' disputing, Simon Peter rose and told the old Nazarite allegory of the rich man and the beggar, which John the Baptist had thundered. Andrew then dismissed the crowd, and Jesus refused ever to comment on this parable.
acts.note.169:3.diff: The Gospel of Luke has Jesus tell this parable himself, whereas The Urantia Book says Peter told it as an old Nazarite allegory not according to Jesus' gospel, and names the rich man Dives.
acts.note.169:4.desc: Jesus never called the Father a king. About the Father he taught chiefly that God is spirit and that he is the Father of his creatures. Men could know the Father by seeing the life Jesus lived rather than by his words, and that evening he declared that he came from the Father and was going back to him.
acts.note.170:0.desc: On Saturday afternoon, March 11, Jesus preached his last sermon at Pella, a full discussion of the kingdom of heaven. Because his apostles and disciples confused the terms kingdom of heaven and kingdom of God and clung to ideas of a temporal king, he tried that day to make his teaching clear.
acts.note.170:1.desc: The Hebrew prophets presented the kingdom as both a present reality and a future hope; later Jews added the idea of a supernatural kingdom, and the Persians that of good triumphing over evil. Jesus always taught the apostles that the kingdom is a personal experience, and his last word was that the kingdom is within you.
acts.note.170:2.desc: Jesus teaches that the kingdom of heaven rests on the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, freeing men from fear and making spiritual attainment the goal of life. He tried without success to substitute 'the doing of the will of God' for the word kingdom, and taught that men enter the kingdom now by faith and hunger for truth.
acts.note.170:3.desc: Jesus teaches that childlike faith is the key to the kingdom's door, but that believers must then climb the steps of righteousness. God's forgiveness is experienced in the measure that men forgive their fellows, and true righteousness is the natural fruit of loving one's neighbor. He taught religion as the cause and ethics as the result.
acts.note.170:4.desc: That day Jesus noted five phases of the kingdom: the believer's inward experience, the brotherhood of believers, the supermortal brotherhood, the hope of a new social order, and the age of light and life. He promised a future revelation of the kingdom and his own return but never linked the two, though the apostles did and expected him back soon.
acts.note.170:5.desc: As Jesus' teaching passed to gentile soil, the Messiah of the kingdom became the Redeemer of the church, and Paul's institutional church practically replaced the spiritual kingdom in believers' hearts. Yet the church is only a cocoon for the thwarted spiritual kingdom, and someday a greater John the Baptist may arise to revive Jesus' concept of the kingdom.
acts.note.171:0.desc: The day after the sermon on the kingdom, Jesus announced he would go up to the Passover at Jerusalem by way of southern Perea, and his followers assumed he would establish the temporal kingdom.
