That Sunday afternoon Salome's request for her sons angered the apostles, and Jesus taught that whoever would be great must be a servant.
acts.sub.171:0.4–7: The request of Salome and the sons of Zebedee
acts.note.sub:171:0.4–7.desc: On Sunday afternoon at Pella, Salome came with her sons James and John and asked that they sit on Jesus' right and left in the kingdom he was going to establish in Jerusalem. Jesus said such places are for the Father to decide and taught the ten about service. That evening, through Peter's efforts, the two brothers apologized.
acts.note.sub:171:0.4–7.diff: Matthew says the mother asked and Mark says the sons asked, whereas The Urantia Book has Salome come with her sons to ask. The ransom saying is absent, and the apology through Peter's mediation is added.
acts.note.171:1.desc: On the forenoon of Monday, March 13, Jesus and the twelve took final leave of the Pella camp and headed for southern Perea, followed by about one thousand disciples. On Wednesday, March 15, acting on Andrew's instructions, David Zebedee closed the visitors' camp, sold its equipment, and later turned the money over to Judas Iscariot.
acts.note.171:2.desc: At the Bethany ford of the Jordan, the disciples hesitated on learning that Jesus was not going directly to Jerusalem. Jesus climbed upon a huge stone and delivered the discourse on Counting the Cost, citing the man building a tower and the king going to war, and asked for dedication even to life itself. About five hundred then followed him toward Heshbon.
acts.note.171:2.diff: The Gospel of Luke says to hate father, mother, wife, children, and one's own life, whereas The Urantia Book says to be willing to forsake them, and sets the discourse on a huge stone at the Jordan ford.
acts.note.171:3.desc: For more than two weeks Jesus and the twelve visited the towns of southern Perea where the seventy worked. At Heshbon Jesus saw Abner for the last time and told him to carry on the work. Though the apostles knew the Sanhedrin had condemned Jesus, the raising of Lazarus left them in quiet expectation rather than fear.
acts.note.171:4.desc: On Wednesday evening, March 29, at the camp at Livias, Simon Zelotes and Simon Peter received more than one hundred swords and distributed them. The next morning Jesus again foretold his death and his rising on the third day, answered the warning about Herod, and set out for Jerusalem by way of Jericho.
acts.sub.171:4.2–3: At Livias Jesus again foretells his death
acts.note.sub:171:4.2–3.desc: Early Thursday morning at Livias, Jesus had Andrew awaken the apostles and warned them not to trust in the defenses of the flesh. He said the Son of Man would be delivered to the chief priests and gentiles, mocked, and killed, but would rise on the third day. Blinded by hopes of a temporal kingdom, they would not take his words literally.
acts.note.sub:171:4.2–3.diff: The Gospels set this on the road up to Jerusalem, whereas The Urantia Book puts it at Livias the morning after the swords were distributed and says the apostles took the third day as a figure of speech for a short time.
acts.sub.171:4.4–7: The warning about Herod and Jesus' answer
acts.note.sub:171:4.4–7.desc: At Livias, just after breakfast, friendly Pharisees warned Jesus to flee because Herod sought to kill him. Jesus told them to tell that fox that the Son of Man would preach in Perea today and go to Judea tomorrow, lamented over Jerusalem that kills the prophets, and said they would go up to the Passover.
acts.note.sub:171:4.4–7.diff: The Gospel of Luke names no place, whereas The Urantia Book places it at Livias and explains that Herod really wanted to drive Jesus out of his domains rather than kill him; casting out devils and healing becomes preaching.
acts.note.171:5.desc: Late on Thursday afternoon, March 30, as Jesus and about two hundred followers neared the gate of Jericho, the elderly beggar Bartimeus, blind from his youth, cried out to him. When rebuked he cried louder, and Jesus called him and, seeing his faith, restored his sight. Bartimeus stayed near Jesus until he left the next day.
acts.note.171:5.diff: The Gospel of Matthew has two blind men as Jesus left Jericho, whereas The Urantia Book tells of Bartimeus alone as Jesus entered the city, adding that he had resolved to seek healing after hearing of the blind Josiah's cure in Jerusalem.
acts.note.171:6.desc: Entering Jericho near sundown, Jesus called Zaccheus, the short chief publican who had climbed a sycamore tree, and said he would stay at his house. When a Pharisee objected, Zaccheus promised to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold whatever he had wrongly taken, and Jesus declared that salvation had come to this house.
acts.note.171:6.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Zaccheus spoke to the Lord, whereas The Urantia Book says he stood on a chair and declared it publicly to the people of Jericho, and Jesus said he had truly become a son of Abraham.
acts.note.171:7.desc: Jesus spread good cheer everywhere he went and never hurried, comforting and helping people as he passed by. Because he truly understood and loved men, he showed genuine sympathy, and most of his important work happened incidentally along the way. His followers likewise must learn to do good in the course of daily life.
acts.note.171:8.desc: Leaving Jericho near noon, Jesus paused for lunch halfway up the road to Bethany and told the apostles the parable of the pounds. Based on the experience of Archelaus, it told of a rejected nobleman who entrusted one pound each to twelve servants and called them to account on his return. Nathaniel later taught its meaning in four points.
acts.note.171:8.diff: The Gospel of Luke has ten servants and ends with the slaying of the nobleman's enemies, whereas The Urantia Book gives the pounds to twelve servants, the apostles, bases the story on Archelaus, and omits the execution of enemies.
